lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Atom: Structure and Sub-atomic Particles

pages.body:
Everything around you — this paper, the air, your own body — is made of atoms. Atoms are so small that a single full stop on this page contains about five billion of them. Yet scientists know exactly what is inside each atom. How? Through more than a century of careful experiments, they built up a picture of the atom's internal structure.

- If you could zoom into a piece of iron until you reached its smallest possible particle, what do you think you would find?
- Do you think atoms from different elements (such as carbon, oxygen and gold) are different from each other? In what ways?

> **DEFINITION** **Atom:** the smallest particle of an element that retains the chemical properties of that element. All matter is made of atoms. **Element:** a pure substance made entirely of one type of atom. Examples include hydrogen (H), carbon (C), oxygen (O) and sodium (Na). **Sub-atomic particles:** the three smaller particles found inside atoms: protons, neutrons and electrons.

[[img:i27c6idx0]]

pages.title: The three sub-atomic particles
pages.body:
Every atom contains three types of particle, each with a specific location and electrical charge. The nucleus is the very dense, positively charged centre of the atom. It contains protons and neutrons packed tightly together. The electrons are tiny, negatively charged particles that travel rapidly in regions called shells (or orbits) at different distances from the nucleus.

The proton carries a positive charge of +1. Every atom of the same element has the same number of protons — this is what makes elements different from each other. Carbon always has 6 protons; oxygen always has 8; sodium always has 11.

The neutron carries no electrical charge (it is neutral). Neutrons are found in the nucleus alongside protons. They help hold the nucleus together. Adding or removing a neutron does not change the element, but it does change the mass.

The electron carries a negative charge of −1. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the positive and negative charges balance out perfectly. The atom as a whole has no net charge.

pages.title: Atomic number and mass number
pages.body:
Every element is identified by two numbers. The atomic number (symbol Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus. This is the most important number because it defines what element an atom is. No two elements have the same atomic number. The mass number (symbol A) is the total number of protons plus neutrons in the nucleus. Electrons are so light that they contribute almost nothing to the mass.

From these two numbers you can calculate the number of each particle in any atom. The number of protons equals the atomic number (Z). The number of electrons in a neutral atom also equals Z. The number of neutrons equals the mass number minus the atomic number: A − Z.

Example: Carbon has Z = 6 and A = 12. It has 6 protons, 6 electrons, and 12 − 6 = 6 neutrons.

Example: Sodium has Z = 11 and A = 23. It has 11 protons, 11 electrons, and 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons.

Example: Chlorine has Z = 17 and A = 35. It has 17 protons, 17 electrons, and 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons.

> **Lesson 1 Assessment**

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Periodic Table and Electron Configuration

pages.body:
The periodic table is one of the most powerful tools in all of science. More than 150 years ago, Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements in a way that revealed a hidden pattern — when elements are placed in order of their atomic number, elements with similar properties appear at regular intervals.

- Have you seen a periodic table before? What do you notice about how it is organised?
- Why do you think elements are arranged in rows and columns rather than just one long list?

> **DEFINITION** **Periodic table:** a chart of all known elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number (proton number), with elements that have similar properties placed in the same vertical column. **Electron configuration:** the distribution of electrons in the shells (energy levels) of an atom, written as a series of numbers for each shell. **Shell (energy level):** a region around the nucleus in which electrons orbit. Each shell can hold a maximum number of electrons: shell 1 holds up to 2; shell 2 holds up to 8; shell 3 holds up to 8.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How elements are arranged in the periodic table

pages.title: How elements are arranged in the periodic table
pages.body: The periodic table arranges all known elements in order of their atomic number — that is, in order of the number of protons in the nucleus. Hydrogen (Z = 1) comes first, helium (Z = 2) second, lithium (Z = 3) third, and so on. When arranged this way, a remarkable pattern appears: elements in the same vertical column (called a group) have very similar chemical properties, even though they are made of completely different atoms.

The rows in the periodic table are called periods. A new row (period) starts each time a new electron shell begins to fill. Period 1 contains just hydrogen and helium (filling shell 1). Period 2 contains lithium through neon (filling shell 2). Period 3 contains sodium through argon (filling shell 3). The group number often tells you how many electrons are in the outer shell, which determines how the element reacts chemically.

pages.title: Drawing electron configurations
pages.body:
The electron configuration shows exactly how many electrons are in each shell of an atom. The rules are: Shell 1 holds a maximum of 2 electrons and fills first. Shell 2 holds a maximum of 8 electrons. Shell 3 also holds up to 8 electrons for the first 18 elements. Electrons fill the innermost shells first before going to outer shells.

To write the electron configuration, list the number of electrons in each shell separated by dots or pipes. Here are some examples to study:

- Hydrogen (Z = 1): one electron in shell 1. Configuration: 1
- Helium (Z = 2): two electrons in shell 1. Configuration: 2
- Lithium (Z = 3): two in shell 1, one in shell 2. Configuration: 2.1
- Carbon (Z = 6): two in shell 1, four in shell 2. Configuration: 2.4
- Oxygen (Z = 8): two in shell 1, six in shell 2. Configuration: 2.6
- Sodium (Z = 11): two in shell 1, eight in shell 2, one in shell 3. Configuration: 2.8.1
- Chlorine (Z = 17): two in shell 1, eight in shell 2, seven in shell 3. Configuration: 2.8.7
- Calcium (Z = 20): two in shell 1, eight in shell 2, eight in shell 3, two in shell 4. Configuration: 2.8.8.2

Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. This is why they behave similarly — it is the outer electrons that determine how an element reacts.

pages.body:
When you dissolve salt in water, the salt conducts electricity in the solution. Pure water alone conducts electricity very poorly. What happens when salt dissolves that gives the solution the ability to conduct electricity? And when two hydrogen atoms bond with one oxygen atom to make water, what holds them together?

- What do you think happens to salt (sodium chloride) when it dissolves in water — does it just disappear, or does something change at the particle level?
- If an atom can gain or lose electrons, how would that change its electrical charge?

> **DEFINITION** **Ion:** an atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost one or more electrons and therefore carries an electrical charge. **Cation:** a positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses one or more electrons. Metals typically form cations. **Anion:** a negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains one or more electrons. Non-metals typically form anions. **Molecule:** a particle formed when two or more atoms are chemically bonded together. A molecule is the smallest unit of a compound or element that can exist independently.

pages.title: How ions are formed
pages.body:
A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so its charges cancel out. When an atom loses electrons, the number of protons (positive charges) becomes greater than the number of electrons (negative charges), and the atom becomes positively charged. This positively charged ion is called a cation. When an atom gains electrons, the electrons outnumber the protons, and the atom becomes negatively charged — this is an anion.

Sodium (Na) has 11 protons and 11 electrons in a neutral atom. Its electron configuration is 2.8.1. The single outer electron makes sodium very reactive — it tends to lose that electron to achieve a stable, full outer shell (like neon, configuration 2.8). When it loses the one electron, it becomes Na⁺: 11 protons, 10 electrons, net charge +1.

Chlorine (Cl) has 17 protons and 17 electrons. Its configuration is 2.8.7. With 7 outer electrons, chlorine is one short of a full outer shell. It tends to gain one electron to achieve the stable configuration 2.8.8 (like argon). When it gains the electron, it becomes Cl⁻: 17 protons, 18 electrons, net charge −1.

When Na⁺ and Cl⁻ come together, the attraction between opposite charges holds them together in a lattice structure. This is sodium chloride (NaCl) — table salt. The ions in salt water can move freely and carry electrical current, which is why salt water conducts electricity.

pages.title: Molecules
pages.body:
A molecule is a group of two or more atoms that are chemically bonded together. Unlike ions, atoms in a molecule share electrons (covalent bonds) rather than completely transferring them. The shared electrons hold the atoms together.

Molecules can be made of atoms of the same element or different elements. Hydrogen gas exists as H₂ — two hydrogen atoms bonded together. Oxygen gas is O₂ — two oxygen atoms bonded. Water (H₂O) has two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) has one carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms. Ammonia (NH₃) has one nitrogen atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms.

The formula of a molecule tells you exactly how many atoms of each element it contains. H₂O means 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. CO₂ means 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms. CH₄ (methane) means 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms.

> **Did you know?** Your blood contains important ions, including Na⁺ (sodium), K⁺ (potassium), Ca²⁺ (calcium) and Cl⁻ (chloride). These ions are essential for nerve impulses, muscle contraction and maintaining fluid balance. Sports drinks contain these ions (marketed as 'electrolytes') to replace what is lost through sweat during exercise.

pages.title: More examples of ions
pages.body:
| **Atom** | **Electron configuration of the atom** | **What happens** | **Ion formed** | **Electron configuration of the ion** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Magnesium | 2.8.2 | Loses 2 electrons | Mg²⁺ | 2.8 |
| Aluminium | 2.8.3 | Loses 3 electrons | Al³⁺ | 2.8 |
| Potassium | 2.8.8.1 | Loses 1 electron | K⁺ | 2.8.8 |
| Calcium | 2.8.8.2 | Loses 2 electrons | Ca²⁺ | 2.8.8 |
| Oxygen | 2.6 | Gains 2 electrons | O²⁻ | 2.8 |
| Fluorine | 2.7 | Gains 1 electron | F⁻ | 2.8 |
| Sulphur | 2.8.6 | Gains 2 electrons | S²⁻ | 2.8.8 |

Metals have one, two or three electrons in the outer shell and lose them to form positive ions. Non metals have five, six or seven electrons in the outer shell and gain electrons to form negative ions. In each case the ion ends with a full outer shell.

pages.title: Atoms, ions and molecules compared
pages.body:
| **Particle** | **Charge** | **Description** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Atom | None | The smallest particle of an element, with equal numbers of protons and electrons | Na, Cl, O |
| Ion | Positive or negative | An atom or group of atoms that has lost or gained electrons | Na⁺, Cl⁻, Ca²⁺ |
| Molecule | None | Two or more atoms joined together by sharing electrons | H₂, O₂, H₂O, CO₂ |

pages.body:
| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Atom | The smallest particle of an element that retains the chemical properties of that element |
| Element | A pure substance made entirely of one type of atom |
| Nucleus | The dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons |
| Proton | A sub-atomic particle in the nucleus with a positive charge of +1 |
| Neutron | A sub-atomic particle in the nucleus with no charge (neutral) |
| Electron | A sub-atomic particle in shells around the nucleus with a negative charge of −1 |
| Atomic number (Z) | The number of protons in the nucleus; determines the identity of the element |
| Mass number (A) | The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus |
| Periodic table | A chart of all elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number |
| Electron configuration | The distribution of electrons in shells, written as numbers for each shell |
| Shell (energy level) | A region around the nucleus where electrons are found; shell 1 holds max 2, shell 2 holds max 8 |
| Ion | An atom that has gained or lost electrons and carries an electrical charge |
| Cation | A positively charged ion formed by losing electrons |
| Anion | A negatively charged ion formed by gaining electrons |
| Molecule | A group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together |
| Electrolyte | An ion in solution that can conduct electricity |
